/-!
# Conjecture 10.75

by V. P. Shunkov

Suppose that a group $G$ contains an element $a$ of prime order $p$ such that the
normalizer of every finite subgroup containing $a$ has finite periodic part and all
subgroups $\langle a, a^g \rangle$, $g \in G$, are finite and almost all of them are
soluble. Does $G$ possess a periodic part if $p > 2$?

The *periodic part* of a group is the set of all its elements of finite order, provided
this set is a subgroup; a group *possesses a periodic part* if its elements of finite
order form a subgroup. "Almost all" means "all but finitely many": only finitely many of
the subgroups $\langle a, a^g \rangle$ are non-soluble.

The notebook remarks that the answer is affirmative if $a$ is a *point* in the sense of
Senashov and Shunkov (Algebra and Logic **22** (1983), 66–81), and that a group with a
point $a$ of order $2$ satisfying the hypotheses but without a periodic part exists
(V. P. Shunkov, *Groups with involutions*, Preprints no. 4, 5, 12 of the Comput. centre of
SO AN SSSR, Krasnoyarsk, 1986).

*Reference:* [The Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v46)
-/

def HasPeriodicPart (G : Type*) [Group G] : Prop :=

A group $G$ *possesses a periodic part* if the set of its elements of finite order

justification.closest_existing_considered: CommGroup.torsion (only defined for commutative groups, where the torsion elements always form a subgroup), Monoid.torsion (a Submonoid, always exists), Monoid.IsTorsion (says every element has finite order, which is a different, stronger property).
justification.name: Kourovka.«10.75».HasPeriodicPart
justification.why_needed: Shunkov's notion 'G possesses a periodic part' (the elements of finite order form a subgroup) has no Mathlib counterpart for general (non-commutative) groups.

@[category API, AMS 20]
theorem hasPeriodicPart_iff :
    HasPeriodicPart G ↔
      ∀ x y : G, IsOfFinOrder x → IsOfFinOrder y → IsOfFinOrder (x * y) := by
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨T, hT⟩ x y hx hy
    exact (hT _).1 (T.mul_mem ((hT x).2 hx) ((hT y).2 hy))
  · intro h
    exact ⟨{ carrier := {x | IsOfFinOrder x}
             one_mem' := IsOfFinOrder.one
             mul_mem' := fun hx hy => h _ _ hx hy
             inv_mem' := fun hx => hx.inv }, fun _ => Iff.rfl⟩
blocks.docstring:
A group possesses a periodic part if and only if the product of any two of its
elements of finite order has finite order.

@[category test, AMS 20]
theorem not_hasPeriodicPart_dihedralGroup_zero : ¬ HasPeriodicPart (DihedralGroup 0) := by
  rw [hasPeriodicPart_iff]
  intro h
  have h1 : IsOfFinOrder (DihedralGroup.sr 0 * DihedralGroup.sr 1 : DihedralGroup 0) :=
    h _ _ (orderOf_pos_iff.1 (by rw [DihedralGroup.orderOf_sr]; norm_num))
      (orderOf_pos_iff.1 (by rw [DihedralGroup.orderOf_sr]; norm_num))
  rw [DihedralGroup.sr_mul_sr, sub_zero] at h1
  exact orderOf_eq_zero_iff.1 DihedralGroup.orderOf_r_one h1
blocks.docstring:
The infinite dihedral group does not possess a periodic part: the product of the two
involutions $s$ and $sr$ is the element $r$ of infinite order.

@[category research open, AMS 20]
theorem kourovka.«10.75» : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∀ (p : ℕ), p.Prime → 2 < p →
      ∀ (G : Type) [Group G] (a : G), orderOf a = p →
        (∀ H : Subgroup G, Finite H → a ∈ H → HasFinitePeriodicPart H.normalizer) →
        (∀ g : G, Finite (Subgroup.closure {a, g⁻¹ * a * g})) →
        {K : Subgroup G | (∃ g : G, K = Subgroup.closure {a, g⁻¹ * a * g}) ∧
          ¬ IsSolvable K}.Finite →
        HasPeriodicPart G := by
  sorry

claims.decomposer_note: Yes/no question (open, so answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ G a ...): hypotheses are p an odd prime, orderOf a = p, for every finite subgroup H ∋ a the normalizer N_G(H) has a periodic part that is finite (equivalently, by Dietzmann's lemma, N_G(H) has only finitely many elements of finite order), every ⟨a, a^g⟩ (g ∈ G) is finite, and 'almost all' of them are soluble, i.e. only finitely many distinct subgroups ⟨a, a^g⟩ are non-soluble; the conclusion 'G possesses a periodic part' means the set of elements of finite order of G is a subgroup (G itself is not assumed periodic or infinite).
claims.reviewer_why: All eight candidates state this slot equivalently (answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ p odd prime, ∀ G a with orderOf a = p, [every finite H ∋ a has N_G(H) with finite periodic part] → [every ⟨a, a^g⟩ finite] → [only finitely many distinct ⟨a, a^g⟩ non-soluble] → torsion elements of G form a subgroup). Checked quantifier order/scope, that answer(sorry) is constrained (True = positive answer, False = a counterexample exists), Subgroup.normalizer, IsSolvable on the coerced subgroup type, and that G is not assumed infinite/periodic. c06 chosen as base because it reads 'finite periodic part' literally via a bespoke HasFinitePeriodicPart (Dietzmann-equivalent to the 'finitely many torsion elements' form used by c02/c04/c05/c07) and has clean API lemmas; I added c01's hasPeriodicPart_iff API lemma and the infinite-dihedral-group test showing the definition is non-trivial.

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Conjecture 10.75

by V. P. Shunkov

Suppose that a group $G$ contains an element $a$ of prime order $p$ such that the
normalizer of every finite subgroup containing $a$ has finite periodic part and all
subgroups $\langle a, a^g \rangle$, $g \in G$, are finite and almost all of them are
soluble. Does $G$ possess a periodic part if $p > 2$?

the subgroups $\langle a, a^g \rangle$ are non-soluble.

The notebook remarks that the answer is affirmative if $a$ is a *point* in the sense of
Senashov and Shunkov (Algebra and Logic **22** (1983), 66–81), and that a group with a
point $a$ of order $2$ satisfying the hypotheses but without a periodic part exists
(V. P. Shunkov, *Groups with involutions*, Preprints no. 4, 5, 12 of the Comput. centre of
SO AN SSSR, Krasnoyarsk, 1986).

*Reference:* [The Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v46)
-/

namespace Kourovka.«10.75»

/-- A group $G$ *possesses a periodic part* if the set of its elements of finite order
is a subgroup of $G$ (this subgroup is then called the periodic part of $G$). -/
def HasPeriodicPart (G : Type*) [Group G] : Prop :=
  ∃ T : Subgroup G, ∀ x, x ∈ T ↔ IsOfFinOrder x

/-- A group $G$ *has finite periodic part* if the set of its elements of finite order
is a finite subgroup of $G$. -/
def HasFinitePeriodicPart (G : Type*) [Group G] : Prop :=
  ∃ T : Subgroup G, (∀ x, x ∈ T ↔ IsOfFinOrder x) ∧ Finite T

section API

variable {G : Type*} [Group G]

@[category API, AMS 20]
theorem HasFinitePeriodicPart.hasPeriodicPart (h : HasFinitePeriodicPart G) :
    HasPeriodicPart G :=
  let ⟨T, hT, _⟩ := h
  ⟨T, hT⟩

/-- A group possesses a periodic part if and only if the product of any two of its
elements of finite order has finite order. -/
@[category API, AMS 20]
theorem hasPeriodicPart_iff :
    HasPeriodicPart G ↔
      ∀ x y : G, IsOfFinOrder x → IsOfFinOrder y → IsOfFinOrder (x * y) := by
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨T, hT⟩ x y hx hy
    exact (hT _).1 (T.mul_mem ((hT x).2 hx) ((hT y).2 hy))
  · intro h
    exact ⟨{ carrier := {x | IsOfFinOrder x}
             one_mem' := IsOfFinOrder.one
             mul_mem' := fun hx hy => h _ _ hx hy
             inv_mem' := fun hx => hx.inv }, fun _ => Iff.rfl⟩

@[category API, AMS 20]
theorem hasPeriodicPart_of_isTorsion (h : Monoid.IsTorsion G) : HasPeriodicPart G :=
  ⟨⊤, fun x => by simp [h x]⟩

@[category API, AMS 20]
theorem hasFinitePeriodicPart_of_finite [Finite G] : HasFinitePeriodicPart G :=
  ⟨⊤, fun x => by simp [isOfFinOrder_of_finite x], inferInstance⟩

@[category API, AMS 20]
theorem hasPeriodicPart_of_commGroup {A : Type*} [CommGroup A] : HasPeriodicPart A :=
  ⟨CommGroup.torsion A, fun _ => Iff.rfl⟩

/-- The infinite dihedral group does not possess a periodic part: the product of the two
involutions $s$ and $sr$ is the element $r$ of infinite order. -/
@[category test, AMS 20]
theorem not_hasPeriodicPart_dihedralGroup_zero : ¬ HasPeriodicPart (DihedralGroup 0) := by
  rw [hasPeriodicPart_iff]
  intro h
  have h1 : IsOfFinOrder (DihedralGroup.sr 0 * DihedralGroup.sr 1 : DihedralGroup 0) :=
    h _ _ (orderOf_pos_iff.1 (by rw [DihedralGroup.orderOf_sr]; norm_num))
      (orderOf_pos_iff.1 (by rw [DihedralGroup.orderOf_sr]; norm_num))
  rw [DihedralGroup.sr_mul_sr, sub_zero] at h1
  exact orderOf_eq_zero_iff.1 DihedralGroup.orderOf_r_one h1

end API

/--
Suppose that a group $G$ contains an element $a$ of prime order $p$ such that the
normalizer of every finite subgroup containing $a$ has finite periodic part and all
subgroups $\langle a, a^g \rangle$, $g \in G$, are finite and almost all of them are
soluble (i.e. only finitely many of the subgroups $\langle a, a^g \rangle$ are
non-soluble). Does $G$ possess a periodic part if $p > 2$?

Here $a^g = g^{-1} a g$, and $G$ *possesses a periodic part* if its elements of finite
order form a subgroup. The group $G$ is not assumed to be infinite or periodic.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 20]
theorem kourovka.«10.75» : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∀ (p : ℕ), p.Prime → 2 < p →
      ∀ (G : Type) [Group G] (a : G), orderOf a = p →
        (∀ H : Subgroup G, Finite H → a ∈ H → HasFinitePeriodicPart H.normalizer) →
        (∀ g : G, Finite (Subgroup.closure {a, g⁻¹ * a * g})) →
        {K : Subgroup G | (∃ g : G, K = Subgroup.closure {a, g⁻¹ * a * g}) ∧
          ¬ IsSolvable K}.Finite →
        HasPeriodicPart G := by
  sorry

end Kourovka.«10.75»

items: 'Has finite periodic part' is formalized literally as: the elements of finite order of N_G(H) (as a group in its own right, i.e. the subtype ↥H.normalizer) form a subgroup that is finite (HasFinitePeriodicPart). By Dietzmann's lemma this is equivalent to N_G(H) having only finitely many elements of finite order, but the literal form was chosen.

'G possesses a periodic part' is formalized as HasPeriodicPart G: ∃ T : Subgroup G, ∀ x, x ∈ T ↔ IsOfFinOrder x (the set of elements of finite order is a subgroup). G is not assumed infinite or periodic, as in the source.
a^g is written g⁻¹ * a * g (standard group-theoretic conjugation convention); since g ranges over all of G the family of subgroups ⟨a, a^g⟩ is the same under either convention.

'Almost all of them are soluble' is read as: only finitely many distinct subgroups ⟨a, a^g⟩ (as elements of Subgroup G) are non-soluble, i.e. {K : Subgroup G | (∃ g, K = closure {a, g⁻¹ a g}) ∧ ¬ IsSolvable K}.Finite — following the decomposition notes, rather than 'for all but finitely many g', which would be much stronger when C_G(a) is infinite.
'Finite subgroup containing a' is H : Subgroup G with Finite ↥H and a ∈ H; ⟨a, a^g⟩ finite is Finite ↥(Subgroup.closure {a, g⁻¹ * a * g}); soluble is Mathlib's IsSolvable on the subgroup type.
p > 2 is stated literally as 2 < p together with p.Prime (equivalently p is an odd prime).

Four short @[category API] lemmas with proofs are included as basic tests of the two bespoke definitions (finite periodic part implies periodic part; torsion groups, finite groups and commutative groups have a periodic part).

reviewer_notes: Final file = c06's declaration (unchanged statement) plus c01's hasPeriodicPart_iff API lemma and dihedral-group test. Modeling choices: a^g = g⁻¹ a g (immaterial since g ranges over G); 'almost all ⟨a, a^g⟩ soluble' read as finitely many distinct non-soluble subgroups (per decomposition notes; the 'all but finitely many g' reading would be unreasonably strong when C_G(a) is infinite since ⟨a, a^{cg}⟩ = ⟨a, a^g⟩ for c ∈ C_G(a)); 'has finite periodic part' stated literally as torsion elements forming a finite subgroup (equivalent by Dietzmann's lemma to finitely many torsion elements). Bespoke definitions HasPeriodicPart / HasFinitePeriodicPart are kept in the problem file; a maintainer may prefer to move them to FormalConjecturesForMathlib since 'periodic part' recurs in Shunkov-school Kourovka problems. The two 'point' variants are omitted; the module docstring records the notebook's remarks about them for context only. Compiles with only the 'declaration uses sorry' warning.

Does $G$ possess a periodic part if $p > 2$? It was proved in (V. P. statement_tex:
Suppose that a group $G$ contains an element $a$
of prime order $p$ such that the normalizer of every finite
subgroup containing $a$ has finite periodic part and all subgroups
$\left< a,\, a^g\right> $, $g \in G$, are finite and almost all of
them are soluble. Does $G$ possess a periodic part if $p > 2$? It
was proved in (V.\,P.\,Shunkov, {\it Groups with involutions},
Preprints no.\,4, 5, 12 of the Comput. centre of SO AN SSSR,
Krasnoyarsk, 1986 (Russian)) that if $a$ is a point, then the
answer is affirmative; on the other hand, a group with a point $a$
of order 2 satisfying the given hypothesis, which has no periodic
part, was exhibited in the same works. For the definition of a
{\it point\/} see (V.\,I.\,Senashov, V.\,P.\,Shunkov, {\it Algebra
and Logic}, \textbf{22}, no.\,1 (1983), 66--81).
